text: Lesson 14 designed around ownership. A support organization is shaped differently — cases start unowned and escalate through tiers. This lesson designs for that shape: a fictional company, Harbor Point Support.

Harbor Point's agents don't own a fixed book of customers — any Tier 1 agent might work any case. That argues for Public Read Only on Case and Account, the opposite instinct from the sales design. OWD isn't a style preference — it follows how the business actually works, and write access gets handled separately, by assignment and teams.

New cases route into queues — Tier 1 General, Tier 1 Billing, Tier 2 Technical. A queue is really a special public group: any member can claim a case from it, and it sits unowned until someone does. That replaces most of the individual-ownership model from the sales lesson.

When Tier 1 can't resolve a case, reassigning it loses context and makes the customer repeat themselves. Instead, Harbor Point adds a case team: the Tier 1 agent stays with read access, a Tier 2 specialist joins with write access and becomes the new owner. Escalate again, and Tier 3 joins the same way. Everyone who touched the case can still see it.

Two sharing rules round it out. Critical-priority cases get routed to Tier 3 with write access immediately, in parallel with the normal escalation path. And Support Managers get write access to every case for quality review, without forcing them into a role hierarchy that doesn't match how support teams work.

Public Read Only on Case, queues instead of ownership, case teams for escalation, two sharing rules for the exceptions. Next lesson turns to restriction rules and scoping rules — two tools that narrow access further, inside whatever OWD and sharing model you've already built.
